title: fastcolab
text:
Most developers know Google Colab as a hosted browser notebook for quick experiments. Underneath that browser UI, Google runs an on-demand CPU, GPU, and TPU compute platform with an official REST API at colaboratory.googleapis.com. You can provision machines, run Python scripts or multi-hour training jobs, transfer files, SSH directly into running virtual machines, and tear down runtimes from code without opening a browser or writing a notebook.
The cost is hard to beat. Google bundles 1,000 monthly Colab compute units into Google AI Ultra 5x ($99.99/month) and 2,000 into Ultra 20x ($199.99/month) alongside Gemini Ultra and cloud storage. Even at standalone Pay-As-You-Go prices ($0.10 per unit), Colab’s accelerators cost a fraction of standard cloud GPU rates. A 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 runs around $0.67 to $0.89 an hour compared to $3.03 on Modal, and a single-chip Trillium TPU runs around $0.41 an hour compared to $2.70 on Google Cloud. If you already pay for a Google AI Ultra subscription, hundreds of GPU or TPU hours sit in your account every month.
fastcolab wraps Colab’s REST API (through fastgws) and runtime Jupyter proxy (through jupyasyncclient) to make that compute practical from Python.

title: fastcolab
text:
Choosing a runtime
Turn on High-RAM (HIGHMEM) on CPU and T4 runtimes. It quadruples RAM from roughly 13 GB to 51 GB and raises CPU cores from 2 to 8-12 for about 0.1 to 0.3 extra units per hour. Every higher accelerator provisions a High-RAM host automatically.
Two paid options are omitted because newer Colab hardware beats them on price and speed. A G4 (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) beats an A100 on every metric: 96 GB VRAM instead of 40 or 80 GB, more RAM, roughly 1.6x higher bfloat16 throughput, and lower hourly cost (~6.7-8.9 vs ~10-13+ units/hr). On paid credits, the Trillium TPU (v6e-1, ~4.08 units/hr) delivers roughly 4.5x the throughput of a v5e-1 (~2.92 units/hr). Use v5e-1 only on the free tier.

Pick the G4 as your default GPU. It has the largest VRAM on Colab, supports native FP8 and FP4, and costs roughly half as much per hour as an H100. Move up to the H100 when memory bandwidth or wall-clock speed dominates and the job fits in 80 GB. Pick the Trillium TPU (v6e-1) for the highest compute per credit when your code targets JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch XLA and fits in 32 GB.
Google does not publish fixed burn rates or guaranteed RAM allocations. Hourly rates vary slightly by region and load. Check live RAM inside any session with free -h.
Colab gives you single-accelerator virtual machines rather than elastic clusters. Each machine attaches one GPU or one TPU chip and caps out at 24 hours even with Ultra or Pro+ background execution. Google can also reclaim an instance when regional capacity tightens. Local disks (~70 to 100 GB) are wiped when a machine stops, so save checkpoints to Google Cloud Storage or Google Drive for long runs.

title: fastcolab
text:
Getting started
fastcolab authenticates with standard Google OAuth 2.0 credentials carrying the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/colaboratory scope (plus https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive for Drive transfers). gclientid automates Google Cloud setup and token refresh, though it is optional: Colab.connect(creds=...) accepts any google-auth credentials directly.

Setup with gclientid
You can create an External Google Cloud project with gclientid. Projects isolate API quotas per person and work with both personal @gmail.com Ultra accounts and Workspace accounts.

Create or update your External project (gclientid enables colaboratory.googleapis.com and declares the colaboratory scope automatically because COLAB is in MAX):

gclientid

Authorize the Google account that holds your Colab or Google AI Ultra credits:

gclientid-auth you@gmail.com --preset colab
gclientid stores one token per email at ~/.config/gclientid/oauth-token-<email>.json. Authorizing a personal @gmail.com account leaves Workspace tokens untouched. Export FASTCOLAB_ACCOUNT=you@gmail.com in your shell.


Setup without gclientid
You can set up credentials directly through Google Cloud and pass them to Colab.connect. See the Colab API documentation and Google’s authentication guides for full details:

Create or select a project in Google Cloud Console and enable colaboratory.googleapis.com (and drive.googleapis.com if you plan to use from_drive and to_drive).
Configure the OAuth consent screen as External (published to production so refresh tokens do not expire after seven days) and add https://www.googleapis.com/auth/colaboratory (plus https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive if needed).
Create an OAuth 2.0 client ID and save an authorized-user token JSON, or mint Application Default Credentials with your project as the quota project:

gcloud auth application-default login \
  --scopes=openid,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/colaboratory
gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project YOUR_PROJECT_ID

Pass those credentials directly into Colab.connect:

import google.auth
from fastcolab import Colab

creds, _ = google.auth.default()
c = await Colab.connect(creds=creds, drive=False)
# Or load a saved OAuth authorized-user JSON file directly:
# c = await Colab.connect(token_path='path/to/token.json')


Starting a runtime and running code
fastcolab wraps both Colab discovery documents, waits on long-running runtime creation, refreshes expired proxy tokens automatically, and transfers files over HTTP or Google Drive.
from fastcore.utils import *
from fastcolab import Colab, outs_text

c = await Colab.connect(account=os.environ['FASTCOLAB_ACCOUNT'])
await c.specs()

async with await c.start('g4') as rt:
    outs = await rt.exec("import torch; torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)")
    print(outs_text(outs))
    await rt.upload(Path('train.py'), 'content/train.py')
    await rt.from_drive('my-dataset', 'content/data')
    await rt.to_drive('content/out.json', 'my-results')
start accepts short hardware aliases ('cpu', 't4', 'l4', 'g4', 'h100', 'v6e1') and enables SHAPE_HIGHMEM automatically where available. Entering the runtime with async with deletes the machine on exit so idle credits do not burn. rt.exec reuses a persistent remote kernel across calls. rt.upload creates missing parent directories and chunks files larger than 32 MB automatically. from_drive and to_drive move files between Google Drive and the runtime using your OAuth credentials, with no interactive browser mount.


Long-running detached jobs
Colab reclaims a runtime after roughly 90 minutes with an idle Jupyter kernel. Spawning a nohup background process and letting its cell exit leaves the kernel idle and risks teardown. rt.launch runs your script inside a dedicated busy kernel cell, logs output to disk, and closes the local WebSocket once execution begins.
rt = await c.start('g4')
job = await rt.launch(Path('train.py').read_text(), log='content/train.log')
rc = await job.wait(poll=5.0, on_log=lambda s: print(s, end=''))
await rt.stop()
ColabJob polls /api/kernels/{id} and tails new log bytes over HTTP Range requests, refreshing the roughly 1-hour proxy token automatically. You can also call await job.status() and await job.tail() directly from another process or after waking a laptop. Save checkpoints periodically to Google Drive or Google Cloud Storage in case the machine hits the 24-hour cap or gets reclaimed.


Fast repeatable environments
Consumer Colab boots Google’s fixed base image (PyTorch, CUDA, JAX, and uv preinstalled) rather than custom Docker containers. Importing fastcolab.envs patches environment helpers onto ColabRuntime for lockfile installs, portable virtual environments, and warm runtime reuse.
from fastcolab.envs import compile_reqs

lock = compile_reqs(['timm', 'datasets'])
await rt.install(reqs=lock, no_deps=True)

await rt.create_venv('/content/env', ['einops'])
await rt.save_venv('colab-envs', '/content/env', 'env.tar.gz')
await rt.load_venv('colab-envs', 'env.tar.gz', '/content/env')
await rt.restart()
compile_reqs resolves versions locally with uv pip compile so rt.install skips remote resolution and installs through uv pip install --system. For stacks that clash with Colab’s system packages, create_venv and save_venv build and archive an isolated virtual environment once on Colab. load_venv restores that archive from Google Drive on later runs. Run inside the restored environment with rt.venv_exec or add it to the live kernel with rt.activate_venv. During rapid iteration, rt.restart() or rt.fresh_kernel() resets memory while keeping /content and installed packages intact.


SSH, scp, and rsync
Colab runtimes expose native SSH through the runtime proxy (wss://{host}/colab/ssh) with no ngrok or external tunnel. The proxy accepts an ed25519 or ecdsa public key (Colab rejects RSA keys) and opens a root shell over binary WebSocket frames.
rt.ssh() (or colab_ssh, from fastcolab.extras) bridges that endpoint through jupyasyncclient’s jac-ssh --proxy ProxyCommand. Calling rt.ssh() saves the runtime’s WebSocket URL and token in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jupyasyncclient/ssh.json and appends a Host colab block to ~/.ssh/config when missing (you can also update ~/.ssh/config from the shell with jac-ssh --colab). It uses ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 or ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa by default, or you can pass identity=.
import fastcolab.extras

rt.ssh()
ssh colab
rsync -av ./data/ colab:/content/data/
ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 colab
Plain ssh, scp, rsync, port forwarding, and Remote-SSH editors then connect straight to the running machine while the runtime token stays valid (roughly one hour). Call rt.ssh() again after refreshing or starting a new runtime to update the saved session.


Usage, shell commands, directory sync, and one-shot scripts
fastcolab.extras also patches operational helpers onto Colab and ColabRuntime for live credit balance, browser links, shell commands, directory sync, remote script or notebook runners, and bulk cleanup.
await c.usage()
rt.browser_url(open_browser=True)
await rt.sh('nvidia-smi')
await rt.sys_info()
await rt.upload_dir('src', '/content/src')

res = await c.run_script('train.py', hw='g4', download={'content/out.pt': 'out.pt'})
await c.stop_all()
c.usage() reads your live balance and hourly burn rate from /tun/m/ccu-info using your existing OAuth credentials. rt.browser_url() opens a live runtime in your browser without allocating a second machine. rt.upload_dir and rt.download_dir sync folders as a single tarball (skipping .git, __pycache__, .venv, and node_modules). c.run_script provisions a machine, runs a local Python file with optional uploads and downloads, and deletes the runtime in a finally block. rt.run_nb executes a local .ipynb remotely and writes outputs back.

title: fastcolab
section: The REST API is all you need
text:
The REST API is all you need
Google exposes two official interfaces under colaboratory.googleapis.com. The REST API handles runtimes, runtimespecs, and getSubscription in v1beta, plus long-running operations in v1. The hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server runs at https://colaboratory.googleapis.com/mcp.
runtimes.create, runtimes.get, and runtimes.list all return a connectionInfo object containing url, token, and expireTime. Sending X-Colab-Runtime-Proxy-Token: {token} to connectionInfo.url connects directly to the runtime’s Jupyter server. Pairing REST with a Jupyter client such as jupyasyncclient gives you live streaming output, rich display objects such as plots, and plain HTTP file transfers.
The hosted MCP server adds four kernel tools (create_session, list_sessions, delete_session, execute_code) with stateless executionId reattachment across 600-second HTTP cutoffs. In exchange, MCP buffers output as text only and truncates large logs. It omits images and requires repeated 600-second requests for multi-hour runs. Driving REST plus the Jupyter proxy avoids those constraints.
Neither REST nor MCP exposes your live credit balance (get_subscription returns only the tier, such as SUBSCRIPTION_TIER_PRO_PLUS). fastcolab.extras adds Colab.usage() against Colab’s /tun/m/ccu-info endpoint to read live balance and hourly burn rate directly from Python.

title: fastcolab
text:
Technical notes
Some other notes:

v1beta and v1 also accept the read-only scope https://www.googleapis.com/auth/colaboratory.readonly when a caller only needs get_subscription, runtimespecs.list, or runtimes.list.
Passing X-Colab-Runtime-Proxy-Token alone authenticates both HTTP and verified wss:// WebSocket calls to connectionInfo.url (no colab-runtime-proxy-token query parameter or X-Colab-Client-Agent header is needed on the proxy). Colab exposes kernelspecs ['julia', 'python3', 'ir'] (name="py" returns HTTP 500, while omitting name selects Python 3), speaks legacy JSON WebSocket frames rather than v1.kernel.websocket.jupyter.org, and emits custom colab_request frames that clients can ignore.
For quick terminal checks without a Google Cloud project, google-colab-cli provides colab --auth=oauth2 whoami and colab --auth=oauth2 usage.

title: envs
text:
Connect to Colab with Colab.connect and start a single High-RAM CPU runtime that we will reuse across every section below.

acct = os.environ['FASTCOLAB_ACCOUNT']
c = await Colab.connect(account=acct)
rt = await c.start('cpu')
rt

Check what tools and packages Google’s base image already provides. Seeing uv and tar present (and zstd absent) sets the defaults for the helpers below.

probe = await rt.exec('''
import shutil, subprocess, sys
def ver(cmd):
    p = shutil.which(cmd)
    if not p: return None
    return subprocess.run([p, '--version'], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip().splitlines()[0]
for cmd in ('uv', 'tar', 'zstd', 'gsutil'): print(f'{cmd}: {ver(cmd)}')
print('python:', sys.version.split()[0], sys.executable)
for pkg in ('torch', 'chevron', 'shortuuid'):
    try: __import__(pkg); status = 'installed'
    except ImportError: status = 'missing'
    print(f'{pkg}: {status}')
''')
probe_txt = outs_text(probe)
assert 'uv:' in probe_txt and 'chevron: missing' in probe_txt and 'shortuuid: missing' in probe_txt
print(probe_txt.strip())

The environment helpers run uv and tar on the remote runtime. _run_cmd invokes subprocess.run on the kernel and prints stdout and stderr. Any non-zero exit code raises RuntimeError.

title: envs
text:
Fast installs with uv
Plain pip install resolves dependencies on the remote runtime and can overwrite Colab’s preinstalled PyTorch with a multi-gigabyte download. Compile a lockfile once locally with uv pip compile to skip remote resolution. uv pip install --system then installs into Colab’s active interpreter in seconds. Pass no_deps=True to layer small pure-Python packages over Colab’s base image without touching existing dependencies.


source

compile_reqs
def compile_reqs(
    pkgs:str | list | pathlib.Path, # Package spec(s), newline-separated specs, or path to a requirements/pyproject file
    python_version:str='3.13', # Target Python version on the Colab runtime
    extra_args:list=None, # Additional flags passed to `uv pip compile`
)->str:
Resolve pkgs locally with uv pip compile and return pinned requirement lines.


Compile a minimal lockfile for chevron (a small Mustache template library absent from Colab’s base image):

locked = compile_reqs(['chevron'])
assert locked.startswith('chevron==')
locked

install writes any reqs input to a temporary file on the runtime and runs uv pip install --system. If uv is unavailable, it falls back to pip.


source

ColabRuntime.install
async def install(
    pkgs:str | list=None, # Package spec or list of specs to install
    reqs:str | pathlib.Path=None, # Pinned requirements text or local requirements file path
    no_deps:bool=False, # Pass `--no-deps` to avoid replacing preinstalled packages like PyTorch?
    quiet:bool=True, # Pass `-q` to keep output compact?
    extra_args:list=None, # Additional flags passed to `uv pip install`
    timeout:float=300, # Command timeout in seconds
)->str:
Install packages or locked requirements into Colab’s system Python using uv.


Install the compiled lockfile onto rt and verify chevron imports immediately inside the remote kernel:

t0 = time.monotonic()
await rt.install(reqs=locked)
dt = time.monotonic() - t0
rendered = outs_text(await rt.exec("import chevron; chevron.render('Hello {{name}}!', {'name': 'Colab'})")).strip()
assert 'Hello Colab!' in rendered
f'{rendered} (installed in {dt:.1f}s)'

Pass no_deps=True to install a small pure-Python package without letting the resolver upgrade anything else:

await rt.install('chevron==0.14.0', no_deps=True)
outs_text(await rt.exec("import chevron; chevron.__file__")).strip()

title: envs
text:
Archived virtual environments
For larger or version-pinned stacks that clash with Colab’s system packages, build an isolated virtual environment once on a Colab runtime (matching Colab’s Linux x86_64 and Python 3.13 ABI), archive it, and save the archive to Google Drive or Google Cloud Storage. Future runtimes unpack the archive back to the same path in seconds and run scripts with {venv_dir}/bin/python without colliding with system packages.
create_venv builds the virtual environment with uv venv and installs pkgs or reqs into it. Set system_site_packages=True when you want the isolated environment to inherit Colab’s preinstalled PyTorch and CUDA instead of downloading them again.


source

ColabRuntime.create_venv
async def create_venv(
    path:str='/content/env', # Directory for the virtual environment on the runtime
    pkgs:str | list=None, # Package spec or list of specs to install into the venv
    reqs:str | pathlib.Path=None, # Pinned requirements text or local requirements file path
    system_site_packages:bool=False, # Inherit Colab's preinstalled system packages (e.g. PyTorch/CUDA)?
    no_deps:bool=False, # Pass `--no-deps` when installing into the venv?
    quiet:bool=True, # Pass `-q` to `uv`?
    extra_args:list=None, # Extra flags for `uv pip install`
    timeout:float=600, # Command timeout in seconds
)->str:
Create an isolated virtual environment on rt with uv and install packages into it.


venv_exec runs Python directly under {venv_dir}/bin/python for full interpreter isolation. activate_venv prepends the venv’s site-packages directory onto sys.path inside the active Jupyter kernel when you want interactive cells to import from it directly.


source

ColabRuntime.activate_venv
async def activate_venv(
    venv_dir:str='/content/env', # Path to the virtual environment on the runtime
)->str:
Prepend {venv_dir}’s site-packages onto sys.path inside the active Jupyter kernel.




source

ColabRuntime.venv_exec
async def venv_exec(
    code:str, # Python source to run inside the virtual environment
    venv_dir:str='/content/env', # Path to the virtual environment on the runtime
    timeout:float=None, # Execution timeout in seconds
)->str:
Run Python code using {venv_dir}/bin/python for complete isolation from Colab’s base packages.


Create an isolated virtual environment at /content/demo_env containing shortuuid, then verify it runs inside venv_exec while staying invisible to Colab’s base Python:

await rt.create_venv('/content/demo_env', pkgs=['shortuuid'])
iso_out = (await rt.venv_exec("import shortuuid; print(len(shortuuid.uuid()))", '/content/demo_env')).strip()
base_check = outs_text(await rt.exec("try:\n  import shortuuid\n  print('leaked')\nexcept ImportError:\n  print('isolated')")).strip()
test_eq(iso_out, '22')
test_eq(base_check, 'isolated')
dict(venv_uuid_len=iso_out, base_python=base_check)

pack_venv and unpack_venv archive and restore a virtual environment with tar. They default to gzip (.tar.gz) because Colab omits zstd. Passing a .zst filename switches to --zstd when you have installed zstd on the runtime. Unpacking back to the original path keeps virtual environment symlinks and script shebangs valid.


source

ColabRuntime.unpack_venv
async def unpack_venv(
    archive:str='/content/env.tar.gz', # Archive path on the runtime (`.tar.gz` or `.tar.zst`)
    dest:str='/content/env', # Destination directory (match the original `venv_dir` path)
    timeout:float=600, # Command timeout in seconds
)->str:
Extract archive into dest, replacing any existing directory at dest.




source

ColabRuntime.pack_venv
async def pack_venv(
    venv_dir:str='/content/env', # Virtual environment directory on the runtime
    archive:str='/content/env.tar.gz', # Output archive path on the runtime (`.tar.gz` or `.tar.zst`)
    timeout:float=600, # Command timeout in seconds
)->str:
Compress venv_dir into archive on the runtime.


Pack /content/demo_env locally on the runtime and check the compressed size:

await rt.pack_venv('/content/demo_env', '/content/demo_env.tar.gz')
sz = outs_text(await rt.exec("import os; f'{os.path.getsize(\"/content/demo_env.tar.gz\")/1024:.1f} KB'")).strip()
await _run_cmd(rt, ['rm', '-f', '/content/demo_env.tar.gz'])
sz

save_venv and load_venv wrap pack_venv and unpack_venv around to_drive and from_drive for one-call Google Drive persistence. For multi-gigabyte environments, use gsutil cp with a Google Cloud Storage bucket instead. Colab includes gsutil, and transfers stay inside Google’s network.


source

ColabRuntime.load_venv
async def load_venv(
    folder:str, # Source Google Drive folder name, path, or folder ID
    name:str='env.tar.gz', # Archive filename in Drive
    dest:str='/content/env', # Destination virtual environment directory on the runtime
    timeout:float=600, # Unpack timeout in seconds
)->str:
Download name from Google Drive folder and extract it into dest.




source

ColabRuntime.save_venv
async def save_venv(
    folder:str, # Destination Google Drive folder name, path, or folder ID
    venv_dir:str='/content/env', # Virtual environment directory to archive
    name:str='env.tar.gz', # Archive filename stored in Drive
    create_folder:bool=True, # Create the Drive folder if missing?
    timeout:float=600, # Pack timeout in seconds
)->dict:
Pack venv_dir and upload the archive to Google Drive folder.


Save /content/demo_env to a temporary Google Drive folder, then delete /content/demo_env on the runtime. Restore it from Drive and test both venv_exec and live kernel imports via activate_venv.

env_folder = f'fastcolab-env-demo-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}'
saved_env = await rt.save_venv(env_folder, '/content/demo_env', name='demo_env.tar.gz')
saved_env


await _run_cmd(rt, ['rm', '-rf', '/content/demo_env'])
t0 = time.monotonic()
await rt.load_venv(env_folder, name='demo_env.tar.gz', dest='/content/demo_env')
restore_s = time.monotonic() - t0
restored_out = (await rt.venv_exec("import shortuuid; print(len(shortuuid.uuid()))", '/content/demo_env')).strip()
test_eq(restored_out, '22')
site_dir = await rt.activate_venv('/content/demo_env')
kernel_out = outs_text(await rt.exec("import shortuuid; len(shortuuid.uuid())")).strip()
test_eq(kernel_out, '22')
dict(restore_seconds=round(restore_s, 2), site_dir=site_dir, kernel_uuid_len=kernel_out)

Delete the temporary Drive folder so we leave Drive tidy:

env_fid = await _drive_folder_id(c.drive, env_folder, create=False)
await c.drive.files.delete(file_id=env_fid)

title: envs
text:
Reusing a warm runtime
Deleting a runtime wipes every installed package and everything under /content. During rapid iteration, restart the Jupyter kernel (or open a fresh one on the same runtime) instead. Restarting clears Python memory, variables, and GPU VRAM in seconds. Installed packages, unpacked virtual environments, and /content files stay warm for up to 24 hours.


source

ColabRuntime.fresh_kernel
async def fresh_kernel(
    timeout:float=60, # Connection timeout in seconds
):
Shut down rt’s current default kernel and open a brand-new kernel on the same runtime.




source

ColabRuntime.restart
async def restart(
    timeout:float=60, # Timeout in seconds waiting for the restarted kernel
)->None:
Restart rt’s default Jupyter kernel without destroying the runtime or /content.


Set a variable in memory and write a file to /content, then call rt.restart(). The in-memory variable disappears while /content/warm.txt, chevron, and /content/demo_env remain on disk.

await rt.exec("marker = 'before-restart'; open('/content/warm.txt', 'w').write('persisted')")
old_kid = rt._kc.kernel_id
t0 = time.monotonic()
await rt.restart()
restart_s = time.monotonic() - t0
check = outs_text(await rt.exec('''
import chevron
try:
    marker
    var_state = 'still-set'
except NameError:
    var_state = 'cleared'
disk_state = open('/content/warm.txt').read()
print(f'{var_state}|{disk_state}|{chevron.render("{{x}}", {"x": "ok"})}')
''')).strip()
test_eq(check, 'cleared|persisted|ok')
dict(restart_seconds=round(restart_s, 2), same_kernel_id=(rt._kc.kernel_id == old_kid), check=check)

fresh_kernel shuts down the current kernel and opens a new kernel ID on the same warm runtime:

kc2 = await rt.fresh_kernel()
assert kc2.kernel_id != old_kid
warm_after = outs_text(await rt.exec("open('/content/warm.txt').read()")).strip()
assert 'persisted' in warm_after
dict(old_kernel=old_kid, new_kernel=kc2.kernel_id, disk_file=warm_after)

title: envs
text:
Cleaning up
Idle runtimes continue burning compute units. Delete the runtime once work ends and check that none remain active.

await rt.stop()
remaining = await c.runtimes()
test_eq(remaining, [])
remaining

title: extras
text: These helpers extend fastcolab.core. Two call Colab’s older /tun/m/ endpoints for account balances and browser links absent from v1beta. The rest wire up SSH via jupyasyncclient.ssh, shell commands, hardware checks, directory syncing, remote notebooks, and ephemeral scripts.

title: extras
section: Live compute unit balance and burn rate
text:
Live compute unit balance and burn rate
Colab’s v1beta REST API returns only your subscription tier (SUBSCRIPTION_TIER_PRO_PLUS). Live credit balance and hourly burn rate live on Colab’s older tunnel backend at https://colab.research.google.com/tun/m/ccu-info. Every response starts with )]}'\n to prevent cross-site script inclusion. _tunnel_get refreshes stale credentials, sends authuser=0 and X-Colab-Client-Agent, and strips that prefix.
ColabUsage wraps the raw ccu-info fields in short snake_case properties and renders a compact summary in notebooks. Colab.usage calls /tun/m/ccu-info using the credentials already attached to Colab.


source

Colab.usage
async def usage()->__main__.ColabUsage:
Fetch live compute unit balance, hourly burn rate, and eligible accelerators from /tun/m/ccu-info.




source

ColabUsage
def ColabUsage(
    *args, **kwargs
):
Account-level Colab compute unit balance, hourly burn rate, and eligible hardware.


Connect to Colab and check the live balance before starting a server. gclientid’s colab preset already grants userinfo.email alongside colaboratory. Your existing token works with no extra sign-in.

acct = os.environ['FASTCOLAB_ACCOUNT']
c = await Colab.connect(account=acct, drive=False)
u0 = await c.usage()
assert u0.balance >= 0
u0

title: extras
section: Opening a live runtime in the browser
text:
Opening a live runtime in the browser
Runtimes from v1beta.runtimes have r-... IDs. Colab’s web UI expects the shorter /tun/m/ backend ID (m-...). endpoint decodes that ID from the aud claim inside rt.token’s JWT payload (falling back to the proxy hostname) with no extra request. browser_url builds a link with both ?dbu= and the unencoded #datalabBackendUrl= fragment. Opening it attaches your browser directly to the running virtual machine.


source

ColabRuntime.browser_url
def browser_url(
    host:str='https://colab.research.google.com', # Colab frontend origin
    open_browser:bool=False, # Also open the URL in the default browser?
)->str:
Return a Colab browser URL that attaches directly to this running virtual machine.




source

ColabRuntime.endpoint
def endpoint()->str:
Return the /tun/m/ backend endpoint ID embedded in this runtime’s proxy token or URL.


Start a High-RAM CPU runtime to exercise the rest of this notebook. Calling usage() again shows the active assignment count and hourly burn rate update right away.

rt = await c.start('cpu')
u1 = await c.usage()
assert u1.assignments_count >= u0.assignments_count
assert rt.endpoint.startswith('m-')
link = rt.browser_url()
assert f'/tun/m/{rt.endpoint}' in link and '#datalabBackendUrl=' in link
dict(endpoint=rt.endpoint, rate_hourly=u1.rate_hourly, active=u1.assignments_count, url=link)

title: extras
text:
Connecting over SSH
Colab runtimes accept native SSH over wss://{host}/colab/ssh through jupyasyncclient’s jac-ssh --proxy ProxyCommand. colab_ssh saves a fastcolab runtime’s WebSocket URL, headers, and metadata in jupyasyncclient.ssh’s session store ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jupyasyncclient/ssh.json) and appends a Host block to ~/.ssh/config when missing (or updates it with replace=True). Plain ssh, scp, rsync, and Remote-SSH then work directly with no google-colab-cli dependency. Colab rejects RSA keys; jac-ssh picks ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 or ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa automatically.


source

ColabRuntime.ssh
def ssh(
    *,
    rt:fastcolab.core.ColabRuntime=None, # Optional live `ColabRuntime` to register in the `jupyasyncclient.ssh` session store
    host:str='colab', # SSH Host alias and session store key
    ssh_config:str | pathlib.Path='~/.ssh/config', # OpenSSH config file to update if `host` is missing
    identity:str=None, # Optional `ed25519`/`ecdsa` key path (auto-detected if omitted)
    store:str | pathlib.Path=None, # Optional session store path (defaults to `jupyasyncclient.ssh` store)
    replace:bool=False, # Replace an existing `Host <host>` block in `ssh_config`
)->str:
Register this runtime for SSH and ensure Host <host> exists in ~/.ssh/config.




source

colab_ssh
def colab_ssh(
    rt:fastcolab.core.ColabRuntime=None, # Optional live `ColabRuntime` to register in the `jupyasyncclient.ssh` session store
    host:str='colab', # SSH Host alias and session store key
    ssh_config:str | pathlib.Path='~/.ssh/config', # OpenSSH config file to update if `host` is missing
    identity:str=None, # Optional `ed25519`/`ecdsa` key path (auto-detected if omitted)
    store:str | pathlib.Path=None, # Optional session store path (defaults to `jupyasyncclient.ssh` store)
    replace:bool=False, # Replace an existing `Host <host>` block in `ssh_config`
)->str:
Register rt with jac-ssh and add a Host entry to ~/.ssh/config if missing.


Check idempotency on a temporary SSH config, then register rt with rt.ssh() and verify the stored session matches rt.endpoint.

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='fastcolab-ssh-') as td:
    tmp_cfg = Path(td)/'config'
    test_eq(colab_ssh(ssh_config=tmp_cfg), 'ssh colab')
    first = tmp_cfg.read_text()
    assert 'Host colab' in first and 'ProxyCommand ' in first
    colab_ssh(ssh_config=tmp_cfg)
    test_eq(tmp_cfg.read_text(), first)


cmd = rt.ssh()
sess = get_ssh_session('colab')
test_eq(cmd, 'ssh colab')
test_eq(sess.endpoint, rt.endpoint)
dict(cmd=cmd, endpoint=sess.endpoint)

title: extras
text:
Shell commands and hardware inspection
Running shell commands directly through rt.exec means repeating subprocess.run boilerplate every time. sh wraps that call behind a unique JSON marker so shell output stays separate from kernel noise. It returns AttrDict(returncode, stdout, stderr) and raises RuntimeError on non-zero exits when check=True.


source

ColabRuntime.sh
async def sh(
    cmd:str | list, # Shell command string (`shell=True`) or argv list (`shell=False`)
    cwd:str=None, # Working directory on the runtime
    env:dict=None, # Extra environment variables merged with the runtime environment
    check:bool=True, # Raise `RuntimeError` when the command exits non-zero?
    timeout:float=None, # Execution timeout in seconds
)->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
Run a shell command on the runtime and return AttrDict(returncode, stdout, stderr).


Verify sh with a string command, an argv list, and check=False on a non-zero exit code:

r_ok = await rt.sh('uname -sr && which uv')
assert r_ok.returncode == 0 and 'Linux' in r_ok.stdout
r_fail = await rt.sh(['false'], check=False)
test_eq(r_fail.returncode, 1)
r_ok.stdout.strip()

Colab does not publish guaranteed RAM or disk quotas, and hardware varies by region. sys_info queries the live machine in one call for Python version, CPU count, RAM, /content disk space, GPUs (nvidia-smi), and TPU settings.


source

ColabRuntime.sys_info
async def sys_info()->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
Return live Python, CPU, RAM, disk, GPU, and TPU details for this runtime.



info = await rt.sys_info()
assert info.cpus >= 2 and info.ram_gb > 10 and info.disk_gb > 20
info

title: extras
text:
Syncing directories
Uploading a directory tree file by file over /api/contents requires one HTTP request per directory and file. upload_dir packs the local directory into one .tar.gz archive, uploads it with rt.upload (reusing 00_core’s 32 MB chunking), and extracts it remotely. DEFAULT_EXCLUDES skips Git metadata, virtual environments, caches, and .DS_Store files.


source

ColabRuntime.upload_dir
async def upload_dir(
    local_dir:str | pathlib.Path, # Local directory to archive and upload
    remote_dir:str='/content/work', # Destination directory on the runtime
    exclude:tuple=('.git', '__pycache__', '.venv', '.ipynb_checkpoints', 'node_modules', '.DS_Store', '*.pyc'), # Basename or glob patterns to skip
    clear:bool=False, # Remove existing contents of `remote_dir` before extracting?
    timeout:float=300, # Extraction timeout in seconds
)->str:
Archive local_dir into a .tar.gz, upload it once, and extract it into remote_dir.


download_dir runs the reverse. It archives remote_dir into /tmp, fetches it via rt.download, and removes the remote archive. Local extraction uses filter='data' to keep paths inside local_dir.


source

ColabRuntime.download_dir
async def download_dir(
    remote_dir:str, # Directory on the runtime to archive and download
    local_dir:str | pathlib.Path, # Local destination directory
    exclude:tuple=('.git', '__pycache__', '.venv', '.ipynb_checkpoints', 'node_modules', '.DS_Store', '*.pyc'), # Basename or glob patterns to skip
    timeout:float=300, # Archiving timeout in seconds
)->pathlib.Path:
Archive remote_dir on the runtime, download it once, and unpack into local_dir.


Upload a nested local directory that also holds an ignored __pycache__ file. Then write a new file remotely and download the directory back locally.

td = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='fastcolab-sync-')
src, dst = Path(td.name)/'src', Path(td.name)/'dst'
(src/'sub').mkdir(parents=True)
(src/'sub'/'hello.txt').write_text('hello from mac')
(src/'__pycache__').mkdir()
(src/'__pycache__'/'skip.pyc').write_bytes(b'ignore')
await rt.upload_dir(src, '/content/sync_demo', clear=True)
(await rt.sh('find /content/sync_demo -type f | sort')).stdout.strip()


await rt.sh(['python3', '-c', "open('/content/sync_demo/result.txt', 'w').write('computed on colab')"])
await rt.download_dir('/content/sync_demo', dst)
test_eq((dst/'sub'/'hello.txt').read_text(), 'hello from mac')
test_eq((dst/'result.txt').read_text(), 'computed on colab')
assert not (dst/'__pycache__').exists()
synced = sorted(p.relative_to(dst).as_posix() for p in dst.rglob('*') if p.is_file())
td.cleanup()
synced

title: extras
section: Running local scripts and notebooks remotely
text:
Running local scripts and notebooks remotely
Running a local .py file on a Colab kernel needs four small adjustments. _script_payload strips any #! shebang, sets __file__ and sys.argv, applies temporary os.environ values before restoring them, and treats SystemExit(0) as a clean exit rather than a traceback. ColabRuntime.run_script parses the exit marker and raises on non-zero exits when check=True.


source

ColabRuntime.run_script
async def run_script(
    script:str | pathlib.Path, # Local path to a Python script
    args:list=None, # Command-line arguments exposed as `sys.argv[1:]`
    env:dict=None, # Temporary environment variables for the script
    check:bool=True, # Raise `RuntimeError` on unhandled exception or non-zero `SystemExit`?
    timeout:float=None, # Execution timeout in seconds
)->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
Run a local Python script on this runtime and return AttrDict(returncode, text, outputs).


Run a local script that starts with a shebang, reads sys.argv and an environment variable, and exits explicitly via sys.exit(0):

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='fastcolab-script-') as td:
    sp = Path(td)/'calc.py'
    sp.write_text('#!/usr/bin/env python3\nimport os, sys\nprint(int(sys.argv[1]) * int(os.environ["MULT"]))\nsys.exit(0)\n')
    sr = await rt.run_script(sp, args=['7'], env={'MULT': '6'})
test_eq(sr.returncode, 0)
test_eq(sr.text.strip(), '42')
sr

run_nb opens a fresh remote kernel and executes each code cell of a local notebook in order. It writes the real Jupyter outputs back onto every cell, shuts down the temporary kernel on exit, and optionally saves the result to out_path.


source

ColabRuntime.run_nb
async def run_nb(
    nb_path:str | pathlib.Path, # Local `.ipynb` path to execute remotely
    out_path:str | pathlib.Path=None, # Optional output `.ipynb` path (can match `nb_path` to save in place)
    allow_errors:bool=False, # Continue running later cells after a cell raises?
    timeout:float=None, # Per-cell execution timeout in seconds
)->fastcore.nbio.Notebook:
Execute a local notebook on a fresh remote kernel, storing outputs on each code cell.


Create a two-cell notebook locally and run it on rt. Inspect the saved output:

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='fastcolab-nb-') as td:
    inp, outp = Path(td)/'in.ipynb', Path(td)/'out.ipynb'
    write_nb(new_nb([mk_cell('x = 21'), mk_cell('x * 2')]), inp)
    executed = await rt.run_nb(inp, out_path=outp)
    saved = read_nb(outp)
    res_txt = outs_text(saved.cells[1].outputs).strip()
test_eq(res_txt, '42')
res_txt

Colab.run_script matches colab run. It provisions a runtime, uploads optional files or directories, executes the script, and downloads requested artifacts. A finally block deletes the runtime unless keep=True.


source

Colab.run_script
async def run_script(
    script:str | pathlib.Path, # Local path to a Python script
    hw:str | dict='cpu', # Hardware alias or raw `runtimeSpec` dict
    high_mem:bool=True, # Request `SHAPE_HIGHMEM` when supported?
    args:list=None, # Command-line arguments exposed as `sys.argv[1:]`
    env:dict=None, # Temporary environment variables for the script
    upload:dict=None, # Mapping `{local_path: remote_path}` of files or directories to upload first
    download:dict=None, # Mapping `{remote_path: local_path}` of files or directories to download after
    keep:bool=False, # Keep the runtime alive after finishing instead of deleting it?
    check:bool=True, # Raise `RuntimeError` on non-zero exit?
    timeout:float=None, # Execution timeout in seconds
)->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
Provision a runtime, run a local script with optional uploads and artifact downloads, and clean up.


Run an ephemeral job on a fresh CPU runtime. This uploads in.txt, transforms it remotely, downloads out.txt, and deletes the runtime on exit.

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='fastcolab-run-') as td:
    td = Path(td)
    (td/'in.txt').write_text('fastcolab')
    sp = td/'job.py'
    sp.write_text("from pathlib import Path\nPath('/content/out.txt').write_text(Path('/content/in.txt').read_text().upper())\nprint('done')\n")
    ephem = await c.run_script(sp, hw='cpu', upload={td/'in.txt': '/content/in.txt'}, download={'/content/out.txt': td/'out.txt'})
    artifact = (td/'out.txt').read_text()
test_eq(ephem.returncode, 0)
test_eq(artifact, 'FASTCOLAB')
dict(text=ephem.text, artifact=artifact)

title: extras
text:
Cleaning up runtimes
stop_all deletes active runtimes on your account in one call. Pass ids to target specific runtimes, or dry_run=True to preview what would stop without deleting anything.


source

Colab.stop_all
async def stop_all(
    ids:list=None, # Optional subset of runtime IDs or resource names to delete (`None` means all)
    dry_run:bool=False, # Return matched runtime IDs without deleting them?
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
Delete active Colab runtimes on this account and return the matched runtime IDs.


Preview stop_all with dry_run=True. Then delete only this notebook’s runtime (rt) and verify it is gone.

matched = await c.stop_all(ids=[rt.id], dry_run=True)
test_eq(list(matched), [rt.id])
stopped = await c.stop_all(ids=[rt.id])
test_eq(list(stopped), [rt.id])
remaining = await c.runtimes()
assert all(r.id != rt.id for r in remaining)
remove_ssh_session('colab')
stopped

title: core
text: This notebook is the literate source for fastcolab.core, building the library from raw REST calls into a small async client.

title: core
section: Connecting to the Colab REST API
text:
Connecting to the Colab REST API
Google splits Colab’s REST API across two discovery documents under colaboratory.googleapis.com. The v1beta document handles subscriptions, eligible runtime specs, and runtime lifecycle, while v1 handles long-running operations. Because colaboratory is absent from Google’s central discovery directory, fastgws loads each document directly by URL.
Authenticate with oauth_creds from fastgws using the Google account holding your Colab or Google AI Ultra subscription. Requesting both COLAB_SCOPE and DRIVE_SCOPE lets the same credentials talk to Colab and Google Drive with no browser prompts.

acct = os.environ['FASTCOLAB_ACCOUNT']
creds = await oauth_creds(account=acct, scopes=[COLAB_SCOPE, DRIVE_SCOPE])
v1beta = await GWSApi.from_discovery_url(COLAB_V1BETA_URL, creds=creds)
v1 = await GWSApi.from_discovery_url(COLAB_V1_URL, creds=creds)

Both read-only calls below run without provisioning a virtual machine or burning compute units.

sub = await v1beta.v1beta.get_subscription(name='subscription')
sub

{'name': 'subscription', 'tier': 'SUBSCRIPTION_TIER_PRO_PLUS'}



raw_specs = await v1beta.runtimespecs.list()
raw_specs['runtimeSpecs'][:4]

[{'eligible': True, 'key': {'variant': 'VARIANT_CPU', 'accelerator': 'NONE', 'shape': 'SHAPE_HIGHMEM'}}, {'eligible': True, 'key': {'variant': 'VARIANT_CPU', 'accelerator': 'NONE', 'shape': 'SHAPE_STANDARD'}}, {'eligible': True, 'key': {'variant': 'VARIANT_GPU', 'accelerator': 'A100', 'shape': 'SHAPE_HIGHMEM'}}, {'eligible': True, 'key': {'variant': 'VARIANT_GPU', 'accelerator': 'T4', 'shape': 'SHAPE_HIGHMEM'}}]

title: core
text:
Choosing hardware
Google identifies each runtime by variant (VARIANT_CPU, VARIANT_GPU, or VARIANT_TPU), accelerator, and shape (SHAPE_STANDARD or SHAPE_HIGHMEM). Only CPU, T4, and A100 accept SHAPE_HIGHMEM. L4, G4, H100, and both TPUs already allocate high-memory hosts under SHAPE_STANDARD.
High-RAM gives CPU and T4 runtimes four times the memory and CPU cores for roughly 0.1 to 0.3 extra compute units per hour. mk_spec turns it on by default whenever the hardware supports a choice. Passing a raw dict skips the lookup table so new Google hardware works immediately.


source

mk_spec
def mk_spec(
    hw:str | dict='cpu', # Hardware alias (`'cpu'`, `'t4'`, `'l4'`, `'g4'`, `'h100'`, `'v6e1'`, ...) or raw spec dict
    high_mem:bool=True, # Request `SHAPE_HIGHMEM` when the hardware supports a choice?
)->dict:
Build a Colab runtimeSpec dict from a short hardware alias or pass through a raw dict.



test_eq(mk_spec('cpu'), dict(variant='VARIANT_CPU', accelerator='NONE', shape='SHAPE_HIGHMEM'))
test_eq(mk_spec('cpu', high_mem=False), dict(variant='VARIANT_CPU', accelerator='NONE', shape='SHAPE_STANDARD'))
test_eq(mk_spec('g4'), dict(variant='VARIANT_GPU', accelerator='G4', shape='SHAPE_STANDARD'))
test_eq(mk_spec('v6e1'), dict(variant='VARIANT_TPU', accelerator='V6E1', shape='SHAPE_STANDARD'))
mk_spec('g4')

{'variant': 'VARIANT_GPU', 'accelerator': 'G4', 'shape': 'SHAPE_STANDARD'}

title: core
text:
The Colab client
This container holds the v1beta and v1 discovery clients plus an optional fastgws Drive client. We define __init__ and connect first, then @patch each operation onto it beside a live example.


source

Colab
def Colab(
    v1beta, # `GWSApi` client for Colab `v1beta`
    v1, # `GWSApi` client for Colab `v1` operations
    creds:NoneType=None, # OAuth credentials shared with Drive
    drive:NoneType=None, # Optional `GWSApi('drive', ...)` client
):
Async client for Google Colab runtimes and optional Google Drive transfers.


Create a Colab client reusing the credentials we already loaded:

c = await Colab.connect(creds=creds)
c

Colab(drive=True)


subscription and specs query account entitlements and available hardware without allocating anything.


source

Colab.subscription
async def subscription()->str:
Return the Colab subscription tier string for the authenticated user.



tier = await c.subscription()
assert tier
tier

'SUBSCRIPTION_TIER_PRO_PLUS'


specs lists the runtime specs returned by runtimespecs.list, filtered to eligible=True by default.


source

Colab.specs
async def specs(
    eligible_only:bool=True, # Filter to specs the current account can allocate?
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
List available Colab runtime specs as AttrDict entries.


Inspect the first three eligible specs on our account:

avail = await c.specs()
assert len(avail) > 0
avail[:3]

[{'eligible': True, 'variant': 'VARIANT_CPU', 'accelerator': 'NONE', 'shape': 'SHAPE_HIGHMEM'}, {'eligible': True, 'variant': 'VARIANT_CPU', 'accelerator': 'NONE', 'shape': 'SHAPE_STANDARD'}, {'eligible': True, 'variant': 'VARIANT_GPU', 'accelerator': 'A100', 'shape': 'SHAPE_HIGHMEM'}]

title: core
text:
Starting and listing runtimes
ColabRuntime wraps one live Colab virtual machine, exposing its name, hardware spec, Jupyter proxy url, token, and headers. Both __repr__ and _repr_markdown_ keep the proxy token out of printed output.


source

ColabRuntime
def ColabRuntime(
    colab:__main__.Colab, # Parent `Colab` client
    data:dict, # Runtime resource dict returned by `v1beta.runtimes`
    owned:bool=False, # Delete the runtime automatically on `async with` exit?
):
Handle to an active Google Colab runtime and its Jupyter proxy.


Creating a runtime returns a Google long-running Operation instead of the finished runtime. _wait_op waits on v1.operations.wait until done is true. If wait errors or returns early, it falls back to v1.operations.get. Any backend error raises immediately.
start attaches a fresh UUID request_id for idempotent retries and waits for provisioning to finish. If the operation response omits connectionInfo, it fetches the runtime with v1beta.runtimes.get.


source

Colab.start
async def start(
    hw:str | dict='cpu', # Hardware alias or raw `runtimeSpec` dict
    high_mem:bool=True, # Request `SHAPE_HIGHMEM` when supported?
    runtime_id:str=None, # Optional RFC-1034 runtime ID
    version:str=None, # Optional Colab runtime image version
    timeout:float=180, # Seconds to wait for provisioning
)->__main__.ColabRuntime:
Provision a Colab runtime, wait until it is ready, and return a ColabRuntime.


Start a live high-memory CPU runtime now. We reuse this single server through the rest of the notebook for computations, file transfers, Google Drive sync, and detached job polling. The final section stops it.

rt = await c.start('cpu')
rt

ColabRuntime(r-1a19e1fe-152d-4898-b5fb-0dcc53bf4e8d) (VARIANT_CPU, NONE, SHAPE_HIGHMEM), expires 2026-11-22T05:36:30.563937260Z


runtimes, get, and delete inspect and manage existing runtimes on the account.


source

Colab.delete
async def delete(
    name:str, # Full resource name (`runtimes/{id}`) or bare runtime ID
    allow_missing:bool=True, # Succeed silently if the runtime is already gone?
):
Delete a Colab runtime assignment.




source

Colab.get
async def get(
    name:str, # Full resource name (`runtimes/{id}`) or bare runtime ID
)->__main__.ColabRuntime:
Fetch one active runtime with fresh connectionInfo.




source

Colab.runtimes
async def runtimes()->fastcore.foundation.L:
List currently active Colab runtimes.



active = await c.runtimes()
assert any(r.name == rt.name for r in active)
active

[ColabRuntime('r-1a19e1fe-152d-4898-b5fb-0dcc53bf4e8d', NONE, SHAPE_HIGHMEM)]

title: core
text:
Refreshing tokens and running code
Colab proxy tokens expire about one hour after issue and return HTTP 404 once stale. refresh fetches fresh connectionInfo via v1beta.runtimes.get and returns the updated header dict. That matches the refresh_headers callback expected by JupyAsyncKernelClient.


source

ColabRuntime.refresh
async def refresh()->dict:
Refresh connectionInfo via v1beta.runtimes.get and return updated proxy headers.



hdrs = await rt.refresh()
assert PROXY_HEADER in hdrs
list(hdrs)

['X-Colab-Runtime-Proxy-Token']


outs_text pulls plain text from Jupyter nbformat output dicts (stdout, stderr, expression results, and tracebacks).


source

outs_text
def outs_text(
    outs:list
)->str:
Join stdout, stderr, execute_result text, and error tracebacks from nbformat outputs.


Verify plain stream extraction:

test_eq(outs_text([dict(output_type='stream', text='hello\n')]), 'hello\n')

kernel opens a JupyAsyncKernelClient wired with X-Colab-Runtime-Proxy-Token and automatic refresh_headers. Passing kernel_id attaches to an existing kernel without taking ownership. exec reuses a lazy default kernel on rt and returns rendered nbformat outputs.


source

ColabRuntime.exec
async def exec(
    code:str, # Python source to execute on the runtime's default kernel
    timeout:float=None, # Execution timeout in seconds (`None` waits indefinitely)
)->list:
Execute code on rt’s persistent kernel and return nbformat outputs.




source

ColabRuntime.kernel
async def kernel(
    kernel_id:str=None, # Existing kernel ID to attach to, or `None` to start a new kernel
    timeout:float=60, # Connection timeout in seconds
)->jupyasyncclient.core.JupyAsyncKernelClient:
Connect a JupyAsyncKernelClient to this runtime’s Jupyter proxy.


Let’s inspect the remote host specs and run a small computation. Because rt.exec reuses the same remote kernel, variables set in one call stay in memory for the next.

outs = await rt.exec('''
import os, platform
with open('/proc/meminfo') as f:
    mem_gb = next(int(l.split()[1]) for l in f if l.startswith('MemTotal:')) / 1e6
xs = [i * i for i in range(1, 101)]
print(f"Python {platform.python_version()} | {os.cpu_count()} cores | {mem_gb:.1f} GB RAM")
sum(xs)
''')
txt = outs_text(outs)
assert '338350' in txt
print(txt)

Python 3.13.18 | 8 cores | 53.5 GB RAM
338350




outs2 = await rt.exec('len(xs), xs[-1]')
txt2 = outs_text(outs2)
assert '(100, 10000)' in txt2
txt2.strip()

'(100, 10000)'

title: core
text:
Transferring files
Colab’s proxy exposes two file endpoints. /api/contents/{path} speaks the Jupyter contents API (wrapped by JupyAsyncFilesClient), requiring chunked PUT uploads above 50 MB. /files/{path} serves raw bytes with HTTP Range support for binary downloads and live log tailing.
files returns a JupyAsyncFilesClient pointed at the runtime. upload builds on it to create missing parent folders one level at a time and split files larger than chunk_size (32 MB by default).


source

ColabRuntime.files
def files()->jupyasyncclient.files.JupyAsyncFilesClient:
Return a JupyAsyncFilesClient for this runtime’s Jupyter contents API.


List the default /content directory on our live runtime:

[e['name'] for e in await rt.files().listing('content')]

['.config', 'sample_data']


upload creates missing parent directories and automatically chunks files larger than chunk_size.


source

ColabRuntime.upload
async def upload(
    src:str | pathlib.Path | bytes, # Local file path (`Path`) or raw `bytes`/`str` content to upload
    remote_path:str, # Destination path on the runtime (e.g. `'content/data/file.csv'`)
    chunk_size:int=33554432, # Chunk size in bytes for multi-part uploads (must stay under 50 MB)
):
Upload bytes, text, or a local file to remote_path, creating parent directories and chunking large files.


Upload a small text file into a new subdirectory and read it back through files():

await rt.upload('line 1\nline 2\n', 'content/scratch/hello.txt')
await rt.files().read('content/scratch/hello.txt')

'line 1\nline 2\n'


download reads raw bytes from /files/{path} with an optional byte offset. On HTTP 404 it refreshes the proxy token once and retries. On HTTP 416 (when the file has not grown past offset) it returns empty bytes. tail wraps download for UTF-8 log files.


source

ColabRuntime.download
async def download(
    remote_path:str, # Source path on the runtime (e.g. `'content/train.log'`)
    local_path:str | pathlib.Path=None, # Optional local path to write the downloaded bytes to
    offset:int=0, # Byte offset for HTTP `Range` reads
)->bytes | pathlib.Path:
Download raw bytes from /files/{remote_path}, supporting HTTP Range offsets and automatic token refresh.




source

ColabRuntime.tail
async def tail(
    remote_path:str, # Log file path on the runtime
    offset:int=0, # Byte offset returned by the previous `tail` call
)->tuple[str, int]:
Read newly appended UTF-8 text from remote_path starting at offset, returning (text, new_offset).



raw = await rt.download('content/scratch/hello.txt')
test_eq(raw, b'line 1\nline 2\n')
chunk1, off = await rt.tail('content/scratch/hello.txt', offset=0)
await rt.exec("open('/content/scratch/hello.txt', 'a').write('line 3\\n')")
chunk2, off = await rt.tail('content/scratch/hello.txt', offset=off)
test_eq((chunk1, chunk2), ('line 1\nline 2\n', 'line 3\n'))
chunk2

'line 3\n'

title: core
section: Importing from and saving to Google Drive
text:
Importing from and saving to Google Drive
Native google.colab.drive.mount needs interactive browser consent and Colab’s older tunnel endpoint. Because Colab.connect already holds a fastgws Drive client on the same OAuth credentials, from_drive and to_drive copy files directly between Google Drive and Colab without browser popups.
_drive_folder_id resolves a folder name, a slash-separated path like 'datasets/demo', or a raw Drive folder ID. Pass create=True to create missing folders along the path.
Create a temporary Google Drive folder and upload a tiny CSV into it. We will import that file into our Colab runtime next.

demo_folder = f'fastcolab-nb-demo-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}'
demo_fid = await _drive_folder_id(c.drive, demo_folder, create=True)
csv_bytes = b'city,temp_c\nSydney,22\nBrisbane,26\nMelbourne,18\n'
await c.drive.files.upload(media=csv_bytes, name='readings.csv', parents=[demo_fid], fields='id, name')

{'id': '1LlveMseDnT66q0YMQoO514WcMGUOh0te', 'name': 'readings.csv'}


from_drive lists non-trashed files in the Drive folder, downloads each file’s bytes, and uploads them into remote_dir on the runtime.


source

ColabRuntime.from_drive
async def from_drive(
    folder:str, # Google Drive folder name, path, or folder ID
    remote_dir:str='content/data', # Destination directory on the Colab runtime
    names:list=None, # Optional subset of filenames to copy (defaults to all non-folder files)
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
Copy files from a Google Drive folder onto this Colab runtime, returning uploaded remote paths.


Pull the demo folder into /content/data:

imported = await rt.from_drive(demo_folder, 'content/data')
test_eq(imported, ['content/data/readings.csv'])
imported

['content/data/readings.csv']


Now let’s process /content/data/readings.csv on the Colab server and write /content/data/summary.json, then save that result back to our Drive folder with to_drive.


source

ColabRuntime.to_drive
async def to_drive(
    remote_path:str, # File path on the Colab runtime to save
    folder:str, # Destination Google Drive folder name, path, or folder ID
    name:str=None, # Filename in Drive (defaults to the basename of `remote_path`)
    create_folder:bool=True, # Create the destination Drive folder if missing?
)->dict:
Copy a file from this Colab runtime into a Google Drive folder, updating in place if it already exists.



await rt.exec('''
import csv, json
with open('/content/data/readings.csv') as f: rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
temps = [float(r['temp_c']) for r in rows]
summary = dict(count=len(temps), mean=sum(temps)/len(temps), min=min(temps), max=max(temps))
with open('/content/data/summary.json', 'w') as f: json.dump(summary, f)
summary
''')
saved = await rt.to_drive('content/data/summary.json', demo_folder)
saved

{'id': '1hAcPv-5zc8sHLAU9nYrAyJlSOff-VOWI', 'name': 'summary.json'}


Read summary.json directly back from Google Drive to verify the saved file, then remove our temporary demo folder.

resp = await c.drive.files.get(file_id=saved['id'], alt='media', raw_=True)
result = json.loads(resp.content)
test_eq(result, dict(count=3, mean=22.0, min=18.0, max=26.0))
await c.drive.files.delete(file_id=demo_fid)
result

{'count': 3, 'mean': 22.0, 'min': 18.0, 'max': 26.0}

title: core
text:
Running long detached jobs
Colab’s ~90-minute idle timeout checks whether the Jupyter kernel is busy. Spawning a nohup background process and letting the cell exit leaves the kernel idle, risking teardown.
launch avoids that by running your code inside a dedicated kernel cell. A small wrapper redirects stdout and stderr to a log file and writes the exit code to a second file when finished. Once the kernel reports busy, launch closes the local WebSocket (aclose()) while the remote cell keeps running.
ColabJob tracks that detached run over plain HTTP. It refreshes expired proxy tokens automatically and reads new log bytes via HTTP Range.


source

ColabJob
def ColabJob(
    rt:__main__.ColabRuntime, # Runtime hosting the job
    kernel_id:str, # Remote Jupyter kernel ID executing the job
    log:str, # Log file path on the runtime (without leading slash)
    exit_file:str, # Exit-code file path on the runtime (without leading slash)
):
Handle to a detached cell running inside a Colab kernel, polled over HTTP.


Check how ColabJob renders before launching a real run:

ColabJob(rt, 'k-demo', 'content/job.log', 'content/job.exit')

ColabJob('k-demo', log='content/job.log')


launch clears any stale log or exit files and starts a dedicated kernel. Once the kernel sends status: busy, it closes the local WebSocket while the cell keeps running on Colab.


source

ColabRuntime.launch
async def launch(
    code:str, # Python source to execute in a dedicated detached kernel
    log:str='content/job.log', # Remote log file path
    exit_file:str='content/job.exit', # Remote exit-code file path
)->__main__.ColabJob:
Submit code to a dedicated kernel, close the local WebSocket once busy, and return a ColabJob.


Launch a 1.5-second detached job on a dedicated kernel:

job = await rt.launch('''
import time
for i in range(3):
    print(f'step {i}', flush=True)
    time.sleep(0.5)
''')
job

ColabJob('d0c349a7-8b35-40af-bcb7-591ba5a94cc6', log='content/job.log')


tail pulls newly appended log bytes over HTTP Range. status checks the exit file first, then queries /api/kernels/{kernel_id} (refreshing the proxy token once on HTTP 404).


source

ColabJob.status
async def status()->tuple[str, int | None]:
Return (state, exit_code) where state is 'running', 'done', 'failed', 'idle', or 'gone'.




source

ColabJob.tail
async def tail()->str:
Return newly written log text since the last tail call.



st, _ = await job.status()
st

'done'


wait polls tail and status until the exit file appears, invoking an optional on_log callback for each new chunk.


source

ColabJob.wait
async def wait(
    poll:float=1.0, # Seconds between status polls
    on_log:NoneType=None, # Optional callback receiving each newly tailed log string
)->int:
Poll until the job writes its exit file (or the kernel disappears), returning the exit code.



seen = []
rc = await job.wait(poll=0.4, on_log=seen.append)
test_eq(rc, 0)
full_log = ''.join(seen)
test_eq(full_log.splitlines(), ['step 0', 'step 1', 'step 2'])
full_log

'step 0\nstep 1\nstep 2\n'

title: core
text:
Stopping runtimes and context-manager cleanup
Compute units burn whenever a runtime exists, including idle periods. stop closes any open local kernel socket and deletes the runtime assignment. Using async with await c.start('cpu') as rt: calls stop automatically on exit. Attached runtimes (owned=False) only close their local socket.


source

ColabRuntime.__aexit__
async def __aexit__(
    *exc
):




source

ColabRuntime.__aenter__
async def __aenter__():




source

ColabRuntime.stop
async def stop(
    allow_missing:bool=True, # Ignore already-deleted runtimes?
):
Close any local kernel socket and delete this Colab runtime.


Let’s stop the CPU runtime we created earlier and confirm no runtimes remain active on the account.

await rt.stop()
remaining = await c.runtimes()
assert not any(r.name == rt.name for r in remaining)
remaining

[]
